discovery: Quantum key distribution: physics-based secure communication (BB84 and entanglement-based E91 protocols)

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, USA

nominees.name: Artur K. Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84, 1984) showed that the laws of quantum physics, namely the no-cloning principle and measurement disturbance, can guarantee the secrecy of a shared key. This was the first cryptography whose security rests on physics rather than on computational assumptions. Ekert (1991) connected key distribution to entanglement and Bell nonlocality. His protocol turned the violation of Bell inequalities into a certificate of security and laid the foundation for device-independent cryptography and certified randomness. Together these ideas created a new field. Quantum communication has since left the laboratory: it now runs over metropolitan fibre networks, in daylight free-space links, and between ground stations and orbiting satellites. National and European quantum communication infrastructures are now being deployed. Few conceptual discoveries in quantum physics have produced such a direct, testable and technologically transformative capability. The 2022 Prize recognised the Bell tests, and this is their natural complement.
